body.text: A Chinese AI engineer, working out of a dusty office in Nairobi’s Chinatown, once told me that his clients did not value his work. “I did all that hard work, and none of my clients appreciate it,” he said. “They never pay me what I deserve, and if it wasn’t for them [the people funding me] I wouldn’t even be able to eat.”

He and his colleagues upgrade Kenyan companies’ computer systems with Chinese AI tools, for much less than they could earn in China. That raises two questions: who are these entrepreneurs, and who is paying for them?

I conducted interviews with three small AI firms I met during three months of fieldwork in the summer of 2026 in Kilimani, Nairobi’s Chinatown. The firms belong to a larger study of 30 Chinese entrepreneurs, which I carried out as a research project with the Johns Hopkins University East Asian Studies Department, with IRB approval and funding from a Johns Hopkins URSCA grant.

I interviewed business owners who agreed to take part in the study, in Mandarin and more than once; the quotations are translated here. I have withheld the names and information that could be used to identify the respondents, their firms, and their clients.
Chinese AI Companies in Kenya

The core service these three Chinese firms offer is upgrading a client’s computer systems so that the client can use basic AI or work with existing AI tools. Chinese developers such as DeepSeek and Kimi release their model weights openly, so the firms neither build new AI models nor import them from China. They modify an open model (most often Kimi) to fit what a Kenyan client needs. African businesses have access to the same programs; the Chinese engineers’ only advantage is the technical expertise built up in China.
One engineer had just spent a month on a Kenyan grocery store’s system.
“The AI collects data on what people are buying at the store in what seasons, or what times of the week,” he said. “It helps the company handle inventories.”

Another was asked to “install Kimi-based AI in a [finance company’s] system, which would allow the company to use AI to categorize the various investments it held.” The engineers look for clients that already have some computer system and try to upgrade it so that it is more efficient, more capable, or requires fewer employees to operate.

Most of my conversations with the firms concerned the difficulty of bringing AI into a new environment. The most striking finding was the reluctance of Kenyan business leaders to deploy AI. One engineer described a typical case: “I had a good relationship with the younger sales manager. But then we went to the boss of the company, and he was incapable of agreeing to have me work for them.”

Another suggested that most of the leaders he met were older, had established ways of doing things, and worried that a new technology would disrupt them. Apprehension about AI was the main obstacle to winning clients, and to overcome it the firms lowered their prices well below their already discounted offers.

Taking the engineers at their word only goes so far, so it is worth looking at the choice from a Kenyan manager’s side. Labor is cheap and unemployment is high, so the gains from automating are small, and hiring an AI engineer makes sense only at a very low price.

Additionally, the risk of incorporating AI may seem high from the Kenyan companies’ perspective. Internet and electricity outages are part of daily life in Kenya. Thus incorporating AI represents a risk to these companies, making them reluctant to spend even what they could afford and further driving down the price they are willing to pay.
Some of this resistance is easing.
“It was much worse for the first six months when I arrived,” one entrepreneur told me. “But now the bosses recommend me to other bosses.”

Referrals of this kind suggest the firms are slowly building a local reputation. All of the firms reported that, while still lower than what the engineers wanted to charge, over the past year, Kenyan businesses were increasingly willing to pay more for the AI services.

The Chinese entrepreneurs I met in Kilimani typically arrived in Kenya after some kind of failure in China, such as failing the gaokao (China’s hyper-competitive college entrance exam), going bankrupt, or even facing political persecution. Now they run small, successful businesses. That pattern fits Aleksandra Gadzala’s 2009 research on Chinese small businesses in Kenya’s informal economy.

The AI founders I interviewed, however, did not fit that mold. All three hold graduate degrees from prestigious Chinese universities, and they were the only entrepreneurs in the wider study who left a successful career to move to Kenya. Their firms were not thriving either, due to the requirement to keep their prices low. They reported losing money in three or four of their last six quarters, and their profits were nowhere near enough to support their engineers.
Why would accomplished computer science graduates leave stable engineering jobs to open companies that struggle to pay for themselves?
Who Is Paying?

Outside money appeared to cover the firms’ losses. Funding was the topic on which my interview subjects were least forthcoming, and it took weeks of building trust before raising it no longer ended the conversation. All three engineers said they receive money from one main source rather than a mix of revenue streams, but what that source is remains unclear.

The accounts do not line up. The first engineer said his money came from the Export-Import Bank of China (Exim) but later said it was the China Development Bank (CDB), an inconsistency I could not resolve. The second named the China International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA). The third described a “Chinese Technology in Africa Fund,” but I could find no entity by that name. It may be a garbled reference to the China-Africa Development Fund (中非发展基金), a real equity fund run by CDB, though I have not confirmed this.

If so, the accounts are less contradictory. Exim and CDB are state policy banks, CIDCA is China’s foreign aid agency, and the fund is itself run by CDB, so the names differ while all point to state-linked money. But the hesitancy to disclose in each case makes it hard to take their reports at face value, and unlike their profits or what they do, I couldn’t verify their source of funding. Ultimately, the source of funding should be treated as unverified.

The founders’ opacity leaves room only for inference, and the interviews offer a few clues. None of the founders seemed worried about running out of money. When I asked how long they wanted to stay in Kenya, all three said until they had made enough to go back. Their calm suggests a secure revenue stream. The answer is also odd, since it implies the founders expect to make money, which sits uneasily with firms that survive on subsidy, unless their own pay is part of what the funding covers.

The funding also seemed sizable: the entrepreneurs lived comfortably, at least typical of, if not above, the average Chinese resident of Kenya. That is consistent with a stable source of money, though lifestyle is a weak clue. Private investors, family money, or revenue the founders did not disclose could also explain it, but nothing I found points to those possibilities.

There are several reasons an institution might back such firms. It could consider market entry worth the expense, since moving a few Kenyan companies onto Chinese AI might spur later customer growth. It could be working from faulty assumptions, such as overestimating Kenyan purchasing power for AI, and waiting on a payoff that will not arrive. Or it could recognize how unprofitable the firms are and still hesitate to pull them out, because the cost of placing expert technicians in Nairobi is already sunk.
China-Africa and AI

Chinese AI companies remain a few months behind their American rivals, but Chinese AI is more widely dispersed. As of June 2026, more tokens are being used on Chinese AI models than American ones, particularly in the Global South. That’s probably because using Chinese AI is cheaper.

Beijing wants to extend that lead. China’s July 2026 action plan on AI cooperation and development promises wider access to data, computing power, and open-source AI, with a focus on developing countries.

Analysts have argued that energy and infrastructure limits will impact the AI rollout in Africa. But Kenya is ambitious anyway; its 2025-2030 AI Strategy aims to make the country a continental AI hub. Thus, Kenya provides a case study of how China can promote its AI abroad, and what the main obstacles are.

Beijing’s strategy of releasing open-weight models makes Chinese AI more attractive and helps it spread, but my interviews show where that strategy runs into limits. Open-weight models still require a certain level of expertise to deploy, and in these cases someone is paying for that expertise. If the funders are state-linked, as the evidence suggests but does not prove, then China is footing the bill itself, and the firms’ wage costs exceed what Kenyan clients pay them. Demand is limited, the upgrades are expensive, and the engineers who build them command high pay.

The main obstacle the firms described was skepticism among Kenyan business leaders. I expect that to ease as the engineers build credibility and learn to solve problems particular to African markets, and the referrals one founder described point in that direction.

That, however, also creates an opening for American AI companies in the developing world. Regions with limited AI expertise may prefer closed, finished systems that need no customization, because the low price of Chinese open models does not always outweigh the cost of the experts needed to deploy them. American developers may also hold an advantage in credibility – the problem the Chinese entrepreneurs ran into most. For the Chinese firms I spoke with, the Kenyan businesses are paying for the modifications made by the engineers. Thus, each engineer has to build up credibility individually and can’t just rely on the reputation of the model overall. A standardized model – for example, one sold by a U.S. firm – is less adaptable, but it could build trust as managers watch it work for other businesses.

The findings also hold a lesson for Kenya. Many analysts worry that Africa lacks the infrastructure to develop AI, and electricity outages did raise the perceived risk for the firms’ clients. But the constraint these firms exposed most clearly was expertise. Kenya, and Kenyan businesses, would do well to train its own AI engineers, who could then adapt and deploy Chinese open models without outside help.

The engineer who said he could not eat without his funders was describing his own situation, but it’s a good metaphor for the overall situation. For now, getting Chinese AI into Kenyan businesses depends on someone absorbing the cost of the expertise. Whether that cost falls as clients gain trust will determine if open weights are enough to spread Chinese AI models on their own, or if sustained support is necessary.
